name: Lyo.Notification
tagline: In-process publish/subscribe for small domain events. Not durable, not distributed, and not ordered across machines. Only useful when every publisher and handler lives in the same process.
description: In-process publish/subscribe for small domain events. Not durable, not distributed, and not ordered across machines. Only useful when every publisher and handler lives in the same DI container (typical ASP.NET Core host or worker). For cross-service messaging use `Lyo.MessageQueue` (RabbitMQ, and similar brokers).
features: `AddLyoNotification` registers `INotificationPublisher` as `NotificationPublisher` (singleton). The publisher captures `IServiceProvider` so each publish can resolve the current handler set. Scoped handlers work only if you resolve `INotificationPublisher` from the same scope that contains those handlers, which is fragile. Prefer singleton or transient handlers, or resolve handlers explicitly in tests.

examples.title: Publishing

sections.title: Why this exists
sections.text: Use this when a feature should fire in-process side effects without knowing each handler. MediatR-style pipelines (behaviors, open generics, pipeline ordering) are out of scope. You get a marker type, one or more handlers per notification, and a publisher that resolves handlers from DI and awaits them sequentially.

sections.title: Core types
rows: Marker interface. Your event DTO implements it (can be a `record` with whatever payload you need).
`HandleAsync(TNotification, CancellationToken)`. Many handlers can be registered for the same `TNotification`. All are invoked.
`PublishAsync<T>(T, CancellationToken)` dispatches to every registered handler of that `T`.
Default implementation: `GetServices<INotificationHandler<T>>()`, then await each handler in registration order.
sections.trail: There is no built-in stop-on-first-handler or only-one-handler rule. Every matching handler runs every time unless you unregister it.

sections.title: Registration
items: `AddLyoNotification` registers `INotificationPublisher` as `NotificationPublisher` (singleton). The publisher captures `IServiceProvider` so each publish can resolve the current handler set. Scoped handlers work only if you resolve `INotificationPublisher` from the same scope that contains those handlers, which is fragile. Prefer singleton or transient handlers, or resolve handlers explicitly in tests.

sections.title: Publishing
sections.body: `PublishAsync` awaits each handler sequentially. There is no parallel fan-out.

sections.title: Error behavior
sections.text: `NotificationPublisher` wraps each handler in try/catch. On exception, the error is logged at Error level (handler type and notification type in the structured log payload). Remaining handlers still run. Failures do not abort the publisher or rethrow. Notifications are best-effort side effects: log and continue. If you need transactional semantics or fail-closed behavior, call handlers explicitly or wrap `PublishAsync` yourself. `CancellationToken` is passed through to `HandleAsync`. If cancelled mid-loop, handlers that observe the token stop. Handlers already running complete unless they cancel internally.

sections.title: When not to use this
items: Cross-process or cross-pod events → message bus.
Guaranteed delivery / retries / dead-letter → queue + outbox patterns.
Pipelines that must run middleware in order across all handlers → mediator library.
You need mediator request/response (query objects with return values) → this is publish-only (`Task`, no aggregate return value from `PublishAsync`).
